name: HSTS supercookie
plain: A site stores an ID in which subdomains the browser has been told to load only over HTTPS.
meaning: Each bit is a subdomain set to HSTS or not. The tracker reads it back by probing http:// URLs and seeing which upgrade (Kamkar 2015). Safari's ITP and clearing site data restrict it; HSTS is mostly cleared with history.

web.api: Strict-Transport-Security on N subdomains; redirect probing

steps: Set HSTS on chosen subdomains to write bits
Check which redirect to https to read the ID

data.metric: N bit identifier (a few dozen subdomains)

limits.headline: Can try to tag your browser with a hidden secure site ID, though it is limited
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you visit a site that tries it
can: Store bits by choosing which subdomains your browser forces onto https
Check them later by trying plain http web addresses
Recognise a returning visitor until you clear history or site data
cannot: Survive clearing history in most browsers
Work well in Safari, which limits it
Carry much data; each subdomain gives one bit
limits.reach_label: Small ID, mostly cleared by history
limits.differs: Safari limits it. Chrome, Edge and Firefox allow it partly, but it is cleared with history.

story.what_it_is: A site stores an ID in which of its sub-sites your browser forces onto secure mode.
story.for_you: You never see it. Your browser remembers secure site choices. A tracker can set many tiny secure flags like switches and read them back later to see your personal code. Many browsers now limit this trick.
story.for_makers: It is an old trick to recognize people after cookie clearing, and it still shapes how browsers handle secure site lists. Trackers once used it. Privacy teams want it blocked.

use_cases.example: A tracker sets a pattern of secure site flags on a first visit and reads it back to recognize you.
An analytics vendor uses it as a backup ID when cookies are deleted.
A researcher shows how it could re identify private browsing users.
A store ad partner uses it to re identify a shopper who cleared cookies.
A publisher could match a returning reader behind a paywall.
A game site could link repeat sessions of a banned player.

technical_bounds: Needs dozens of subdomains and many requests
Cleared when the person clears browsing data

history.change: WebKit limits HSTS to prevent cross-site tracking (ITP)
